2030.t: Resembles λεπίς (lepís, “scale”) + *-ρα (*-rā), but with unclear morphology. Perhaps both words are ultimately Pre-Greek; compare λεβηρίς (lebērĭ́s, “shed skin”), and see λέπω (lépō, “to peel”) for more.

2028.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kámptō, *kamptos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend, curve”), possibly related to Latin campus and Lithuanian kampas, kumpas.

2083.t: From διαδέω (diadéō, “to bind round”) + -μα (-ma, result noun suffix).

2041.t: From πόλις (pólis, “city”) + -της (-tēs). The ι from the stem of πόλις led to the backformation -ίτης (-ī́tēs), whence the reanalysis πολ-ίτης (pol-ī́tēs).

2070.t: From Αἰθίοψ (Aithĭ́ops) + -ία (-ĭ́a), of uncertain further origin.

2058.t: Etymology tree Ancient Greek *ἄρ- (*ár-) Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-oyétider.? Ancient Greek -όω (-óō) Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Hellenic *-mə Ancient Greek -μα (-mă) Ancient Greek -ωμα (-ōma) Ancient Greek ἄρωμα From a root…

2051.t: An isolated adverbial formation from χώρα (khṓrā, “space”), initially meaning "in another, separate space or place".

2016.t: From either μένω (ménō, “stay, wait for”) or μένος (ménos, “vigor, power”) and λαός (lāós, “people”).

2062.t: Earlier form: Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀩𐀞 (e-re-pa /⁠elephās⁠/). Probably borrowed from Egyptian ꜣbw Ab-b-w-E26 (reconstructed as earlier /ˈʀuːbaw/, later /ˈjuːbə/)..

2038.t: Related to πάτος (pátos, “path”); see there for more.

2018.t: Disputed. * Analyzable as Proto-Indo-European *bel- (“strong”) (perhaps via an unattested *βελτός (*beltós, “desired”), per Seiler) + -ίων (-íōn).

2024.t: From oblique case forms with *drew-, a stem of Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”) (whence also δόρυ (dórŭ)).

2019.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mrətós, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥tós (“dead, mortal”), ultimately from the root *mer- (“to die”).

2080.t: From δια- (dia-, “dia-, through-”) + κόπτω (kóptō, “to strike, cut”).

2097.t: Connected to Latin lurcō (“to eat greedily, guzzle”) and Middle High German slurc (“throat”) by Pokorny, possibly reshaped according to φάρυγξ (phắrŭnx, “throat; pharynx”).

2093.t: From κέραμος (kérămos, “pottery”) + -εύς (-eús, suffix for person concerned). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀐𐀨𐀕𐀄 (ke-ra-me-u /⁠kerameus⁠/, “potter”).

2050.t: From προ- (pro-, “forwards”) + ὁράω (horáō, “to see”) + -α (-ā, action noun suffix), with shift of aspiration from the initial of ὁράω (horáō) to the initial of προ- (pro-); compare φρουρός (phrourós, “watchman”).

2081.t: From δια- (dia-, “dia-, through-”) + τρέφω (tréphō, “to breed, feed”).

2026.t: Variant of κάλαμος (kắlămos), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱolh₂-m-. Or from Pre-Greek.

2031.t: From the Ancient Greek root λαβ- (lāb-), whence λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”), and -μα (-ma).

2077.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ǵelh₂- (“to laugh”) (which Beekes incorrectly reconstructs as *gelh₂-). Cognates include Old Armenian ծաղր (całr, “laughter”).

2088.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kel͏̌l͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to drive”). Cognates include Latin celer, Sanskrit कलयति (kaláyati), and Old English healdan (English hold).

2009.t: From ὅπλον (hóplon, “tool, arms”). Compare typologically the relation of Russian копы́то (kopýto), копьё (kopʹjó).

2079.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dlukús, *dléukus. On the basis of Mycenaean Greek 𐀆𐀩𐀄𐀒 (de-re-u-ko /⁠dleukos⁠/) and Latin dulcis, Beekes suggests that a possible proto-form with initial *dl- may be reconstructed.

2021.t: Neuter gender of δαιμόνιος (daimónĭos, “extraordinary, divine; pertaining to daimones”).

2020.t: From o-grade of the root of γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be born”) + -εύς (-eús, “-er”, masculine agent noun suffix).

2036.t: From ὅς (hós, relative pronoun) + -ιος (-ios, adjectival suffix).

2040.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-der. Proto-Indo-European *polh₁ús Ancient Greek πολύς (polús) Proto-Indo-European *-yōsder.

2078.t: Beekes does not propose an etymology, and leaves its origin open, though notes that the seemingly-old ablaut in the suffix -των (-tōn) suggests ultimate Indo-European origin.

2012.t: from Proto-Indo-European *údteros (“higher; outer”) from *úd (“upwards; away”); cognate with English outer, utter, Sanskrit उत्त॑र (úttara, “upper; higher”).

2087.t: Related to Mycenaean Greek 𐀵𐀨𐀐 (to-ra-ke), a technical word without etymology; probably a loan from Pre-Greek or some other substrate, based on the variant θύραξ (thúrax) showing variation ω/υ and the suffix -ακ-.

2000.t: From earlier ἐνῴδιον (enōídion), from ἐν (en) + οὖς (oûs, “ear”) + -ίδιον (-ídion). The form was later altered to re-align with ὦτα (ôtă), the plural of οὖς (oûs).

2086.t: From Proto-Indo-European *dʰers- (“to dare”). Cognate with English dare, Proto-Slavic *dьrzъ (“bold”), Sanskrit धृषु (dhṛṣú, “proud”) and Albanian nder (“honor, favour”).

2013.t: The formation is similar to ἀκτίς (aktís), γλωχίς (glōkhís) and δελφίς (delphís) but the root is unclear. The word has been connected with ὀδύνη (odúnē, “pain of body”) but the long initial vowel has not been explained yet.
